title: Why Democrats Must Embrace a “Mom Populist” Education Agenda https://newrepublic.com/article/213750/democrats-must-embrace-mom-populist-education-agenda
author: Jennifer C. Berkshire
summary: Jennifer Berkshire reports from the Texas governor's race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa has made public schools central to her challenge to Greg Abbott, framing state funding shortfalls, school closures, vouchers, and state takeovers as a GOP scheme to rig the system for donors. Berkshire calls this appeal mom populism and traces its reach to Republican defectors and to candidates in other states running against vouchers. She describes an intraparty Democratic divide over the new federal scholarship tax credit, with Democrats for Education Reform lobbying governors to opt in while others seek repeal. Berkshire argues that the long Democratic sales pitch of education as the route to affluence has run out of steam, especially amid fears about AI and white-collar jobs. She concludes that Democrats should drop the false promise of college-for-all and embrace public education as a public good that benefits all children.
points: At least 135 Texas public schools have closed or are slated to close since late 2023 amid state funding shortfalls.
Some Texas Republicans, including a former Fort Worth school board member and Trump voter, have defected over vouchers and state takeovers.
The federal scholarship tax credit lets taxpayers subtract up to $1,700 in donations, with nonprofits taking 10 percent before awarding scholarships.
Only two of the 31 governors who have opted into the credit are Democrats.
Berkshire argues the schoolbook response to AI-driven job loss alienates voters with and without degrees.
quotes: Since late 2023, at least 135 Texas public schools either have closed or are slated to close due to budget crises brought on by state funding shortfalls.

Call it “mom populism”—an appeal that centers a full-throated rejection of school privatization and presents the GOP’s increasingly aggressive interventions into local school districts as “corruption schemes” intended to benefit big donors, especially the right-wing oilmen who hold such sway here.

Given the minuscule number of causes that still bring voters together across party lines, opposition to vouchers would seem like a logical rallying cry for Democrats, including those who seek to draw moderates back into the party fold. Instead, the issue is fueling yet another intraparty divide.
For 40 years, Democrats have made the case that education was the surest route to middle-class affluence. Now that sales pitch has run out of steam.
If the ascendant left populists are demanding pitchforks, including higher taxes on billionaires and tech industry profits, their more centrist fellows are relying on schoolbooks
Now they have an opportunity to move on from the false promise of college-for-all, instead embracing the ideal of public education as a public good that benefits all kids.
